sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the February 2026 Class Health Care Support Assistant College Final Exam, Cicely McDonnell College of Health Sciences (12 August 2026), Multiple Choice Questions Q8 to Q27. Q1 to Q7 are not included because page 2 of the paper was not available.

questions.text: Pulse rate of 124 beats per min is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Tachycardia (B) is correct because tachycardia means a heart or pulse rate above 100 beats per minute in an adult, so 124 beats per minute is tachycardia. It may be caused by fever, pain, anxiety, exercise, bleeding, shock or heart disease, and the HCA reports it to the nurse. Tachypnea (A) is a fast breathing rate, bradypnea (C) is a slow breathing rate, and bradycardia (D) is a pulse rate below 60 beats per minute.

questions.text: The most common complication for nasogastric tube feeding is:
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonia (A) is correct because feeds or stomach contents can flow back and enter the lungs, especially if the tube has moved out of place or the patient is lying flat, causing infection of the lungs. Prevention includes checking the tube position, keeping the head of the bed raised at 30 to 45 degrees during and after feeding, and feeding slowly. Nose bleeding (B), vomiting (D) and perforation (C) can occur but are less common and are not the main complication.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of constipation in immobile patients?
questions.explanation: Inactivity (C) is correct because lack of movement slows bowel activity (peristalsis) and weakens the abdominal muscles, so stool stays longer in the bowel and becomes hard and dry. The HCA helps by repositioning, encouraging movement as allowed, fluids and fibre as ordered. A high-fibre diet (A) and increased fluids (B) prevent constipation, and tube feeding (D) is not the main cause in immobile patients, although low-fibre feeds may contribute.

questions.text: Why is humidification recommended when administering oxygen to a patient?

options.A: To warm the gas mixture to body temperature
options.B: To prevent drying of the nasal and respiratory mucosa
options.C: To increase the fraction of inspired oxygen
options.D: To reduce the amount of oxygen flow in the tubings

questions.explanation: To prevent drying of the nasal and respiratory mucosa (B) is correct because oxygen from a cylinder or wall supply is dry and cold, and without moisture it dries and irritates the nose, throat and airways, causing discomfort, thick secretions and nosebleeds. Humidification adds water vapour, mainly when the flow is high or oxygen is given for long. Warming the gas (A) is not its main purpose, it does not raise the oxygen concentration (C), and it does not reduce the flow (D).

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a triage system in outpatient services?

options.A: To refer patients directly to inpatient
options.B: To sort patients based on the urgency of their condition
options.D: To provide laboratory and imaging results

questions.explanation: To sort patients based on the urgency of their condition (B) is correct because triage identifies patients who need immediate care so that the sickest are seen first, rather than by order of arrival. It is not meant to admit patients directly (A), handle billing (C) or give laboratory and imaging results (D).

questions.text: A HCA is preparing to transfer a patient from bed to wheelchair. Which action is most important before beginning the transfer?

options.B: Assist the patient to wear shoes
options.D: Place the wheelchair far from the bed

questions.explanation: Lock the wheelchair brakes (A) is correct because an unlocked wheelchair can roll away when the patient puts weight on it, causing a fall and injury, so safety comes first. The footrests are then moved out of the way (C), non-slip shoes are put on (B) and the chair is placed close to the bed (D, a chair placed far away makes the transfer harder and less safe).

questions.text: When transferring a patient from bed to wheelchair, the wheelchair should generally be positioned:

options.B: Close to the bed at the patient's stronger side
options.C: At the foot of the bed with the foot board removed

questions.explanation: Close to the bed at the patient's stronger side (B) is correct because the patient moves towards the stronger side, which can support their weight and pivot safely with a short distance to move. The chair is placed at an angle of about 45 degrees to the bed with the brakes on. Next to the door (A), at the foot of the bed (C) or behind the patient (D) make the transfer longer and less safe.

questions.text: Which principle is most important when collecting a stool specimen?

options.C: Take the sample to the laboratory after 3 hours

questions.explanation: Prevent contamination of the specimen (B) is correct because contamination (with urine, water, disinfectant or by soiled containers) can give false results and hide the organism causing the illness. The HCA uses gloves, a clean container, avoids mixing with urine and takes it to the laboratory promptly. A small amount is enough (A, about a teaspoon or walnut-sized). Waiting 3 hours (C) lets organisms die or change, so the sample should reach the lab within about 1 hour, and the container should be labelled correctly at the time of collection (D).

questions.text: Which specimen requires strict aseptic technique during collection?
questions.explanation: Blood culture specimen (C) is correct because blood is normally sterile, so any skin bacteria introduced during collection would give a false positive result; the skin is cleaned thoroughly and sterile technique is used. Stool (A), sputum (B) and vomitus (D) contain normal body organisms, so they need clean technique and a clean container, but not a strictly sterile technique.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an intentional wound?
questions.explanation: Surgical incision (B) is correct because an intentional wound is made on purpose for a treatment, such as a surgical incision or an injection. Pressure ulcers (A), burns (C) and abrasions (D) are unintentional wounds caused by pressure, heat or friction.

questions.text: An occupied bed is made when:

options.B: The patient is unable to get out of bed
options.D: The patient is coming from theatre

questions.explanation: The patient is unable to get out of bed (B) is correct because an occupied bed is made with the patient lying in it, using the turning technique to change the linen while keeping the patient covered, comfortable and safe. An empty bed (A) or a discharged patient (C) calls for an unoccupied bed. A patient coming from theatre (D) needs a post-operative bed.

questions.text: What is the main goal of home-based care?

options.A: To replace hospitals in the care of illnesses
options.B: To provide care and support in a familiar environment
options.C: To give patients better care compared to hospital care
options.D: To reduce the workload of hospital workers

questions.explanation: To provide care and support in a familiar environment (B) is correct because home-based care lets patients with chronic or terminal illness receive care and support at home, close to family, which improves comfort, dignity and continuity of care. It does not replace hospitals (A), it is not necessarily better than hospital care (C), and reducing hospital workload (D) is a benefit, not the main goal.

questions.text: Which intervention helps reduce HCA burnout in a home setting?

options.A: Encouraging patient admission to hospital for some months
options.B: Arranging respite care and support groups
options.C: Assigning some tasks to the family members

questions.explanation: Arranging respite care and support groups (B) is correct because respite gives the carer planned rest and support groups give emotional support and advice from others, which reduces stress and exhaustion. Admitting the patient for months (A) is unnecessary and goes against the aim of home care, delegating clinical tasks to family (C) may be unsafe, and postponing care (D) harms the patient.

questions.text: What is the most effective practice to prevent spread of infection in a health care setting?

options.A: Wearing double gloves when doing patient procedures
options.C: Changing uniforms at the end of the shift
options.D: Shake the sharps container to make room for more sharps

questions.explanation: Performing frequent hand hygiene (B) is correct because hands are the main route by which micro-organisms are carried between patients, staff and surfaces, so hand hygiene at the WHO five moments is the single most effective measure. Double gloves (A) do not replace hand washing, changing uniforms (C) has limited effect, and shaking a sharps container (D) is dangerous and can cause needle-stick injury.

questions.text: Which of the following scenarios requires the use of soap and water instead of alcohol based hand sanitizer?
questions.explanation: When hands are visibly soiled (D) is correct because alcohol hand rub does not work well in the presence of dirt, blood or body fluids, so the hands must be washed with soap and water. Before taking blood pressure (A), after touching the patient's surroundings (B) and before serving a meal (C), hands that look clean can be cleaned with alcohol hand rub (although soap and water is used if the hands are dirty, and after contact with patients with diarrhoea such as C. difficile).

questions.text: What kind of environment do infectious agents thrive well?
questions.explanation: Moist, dark, warm (C) is correct because micro-organisms need water, warmth (about body temperature) and darkness to grow, which is why they grow well in body fluids, wounds and damp equipment. Bright, hot, dry (A), dark cool dry (B) and cold, bright, sterile (D) conditions kill or slow most micro-organisms.

questions.text: Good respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette includes:

options.A: Coughing into your bare hands and then washing hands with soap and water
options.B: Covering the nose and mouth with a disposable paper towel when sneezing
options.C: Wearing N-95 mask continuously when infected with a flu
options.D: Disposing used tissues in a soiled linen bag

questions.explanation: Covering the nose and mouth with a disposable paper towel when sneezing (B) is correct because a disposable tissue or paper towel traps droplets, is thrown away immediately, and is followed by hand hygiene. Coughing into bare hands (A) spreads germs to surfaces. An N-95 respirator (C) is not the routine measure for flu, and a surgical mask is used for the infected person. Used tissues must go into a waste bin (D), not a soiled linen bag.

questions.text: What is the correct order of doffing personal protective equipment?
questions.explanation: Gloves, goggles, gown, mask (A) is correct because doffing removes the most contaminated items first: gloves, then goggles or face shield, then gown, and the mask last, followed by hand hygiene. Option B is the donning order (gown, mask, goggles, gloves). Options C and D take off the gown or mask before items that are more contaminated, which risks self-contamination.

questions.text: Which of the following are upper limb bones?
questions.explanation: Radius, humerus (D) is correct because both are bones of the upper limb: the humerus in the upper arm and the radius in the forearm. The tibia, fibula and femur (A, B, C) are lower limb bones, and the occipital bone (B) belongs to the skull.

questions.text: In anatomy, the heart is said to be ............... to the sternum:
questions.explanation: Posterior (C) is correct because the heart lies behind the sternum (breastbone), and posterior means towards the back. Anterior (B) is the opposite, towards the front. Proximal (A) means nearer to the point of attachment of a limb, and superior (D) means above.
